description: This case study examines the practice of flexing capacity, varying the number of staffed beds to match demand, at a large tertiary hospital in South Australia. Sankalp Khanna and Justin Boyle of the Australian e-Health Research Centre and Kathryn Zeitz of SA Health and the Central Adelaide Local Health Network presented it at the 2014 annual conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. Using hospital data, they analysed how well the flexing protocols worked, how flexing affected overcrowding, and how variation in occupancy affected patient flow measures, comparing the results with earlier studies of similar Australian hospitals that do not flex capacity. The conference paper is available online from IEEE by subscription or purchase; its abstract is free in OpenAlex. Coverage is one hospital, not named in the abstract. Caveats: the hospital data are not published and the comparison hospitals come from other studies. Flexing helped the hospital spend less time above critical occupancy, and it did not show the performance decline seen in hospitals that do not flex; the authors also identify improvements to the protocol. Simulation uses: evidence on adjustable bed capacity as a surge lever for hospital capacity and patient flow models. Related records: the WA HEALTH bed capacity surveillance platform (platform-wa-health-hospital-bed-capacity-surveillance) and Portugal's hospital bed and occupancy data (data-sns-portugal-hospital-beds-and-occupancy) track bed capacity at system level.
